papers.title: Cotangent-lift inference of stochastic microbial dynamics
papers.abstract: We study the parameter estimation for the stochastic logistic and Lotka--Volterra diffusions from discrete, irregularly spaced observations corrupted by measurement noise, a setting typical of microbiome time series. For the logistic equation, the growth rate acts as a time change and does not enter the stationary law, so it can be identified only from the temporal structure of the data. We prove that the maximum-likelihood estimator of the Euler scheme, with the observations taken as the states, coincides with the regression of log-increments on abundances used in the literature, and we characterise what this estimator cannot see under measurement noise: for the linearised dynamics, the law of consecutive pairs of observations is invariant along an explicit one-parameter family of relaxation rates and noise levels, and the regression converges to a limit set by the noise. Treating the true abundances as latent, we compute the likelihood with a Gaussian moment filter and show that measurement noise is precisely what couples the filter states across samples. The exact gradient is then the backward recursion of the discrete cotangent lift, whose cost, two to three likelihood evaluations, does not depend on the number of parameters, and we give the covector map of each filter step in closed form. In simulations, the latent estimator recovers the relaxation times, noise levels and interaction strengths that the regression biases, while larger communities require prior information on the interactions. In gut microbiome time series it attributes most of the variability of a dominant genus to measurement noise and estimates its relaxation time at about $64$ hours, with a large standard error.

papers.title: Fundamental Relation between Conductance of Biomolecules and the Fukui Function
papers.abstract: We derive the finite-temperature conductance of a molecule coupled to metallic leads using open-system time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT). Tracing out the phonon bath via Wick's theorem yields an exchange-symmetric collision integral that preserves Pauli exclusion. When internal thermalization is faster than lead escape, as holds in proteins with multifractal orbitals at the Anderson transition, the exchange-correlation kernel projects out of the slow Liouvillian mode, making conductance directly proportional to the finite-temperature Fukui function of conceptual DFT.

papers.title: Mutual Linearity in Nonlinear Population Dynamics
papers.abstract: Mutual Linearity in Nonlinear Population DynamicsMutual linearity, the persistence of affine relations among stationary observables under arbitrarily strong changes of one transition rate, is known for Markov jump processes and chemical reaction networks. We show that generalized Lotka--Volterra dynamics form a new class of mutually linear systems, even though species can go extinct and attractors can be chaotic. Any change to one species' equation acts on the others as one effective press and keeps all abundances affinely related: piecewise across extinctions, and as time averages on chaotic attractors.

papers.title: Chemotactic Horizons Regulate Threshold Dynamics in the Biological Carbon Pump
papers.abstract: Microbial encounters with sinking marine snow regulate organic carbon remineralization, acting as a critical knob in the ocean's biological carbon pump. Yet how the vast diversity of microbes in the open ocean respond to natural chemotactic cues coupling sedimentation-induced flow to microbial encounters in the ocean remains unresolved. Here we report shipboard measurements of microbial motility around freshly collected marine snow under imposed flows spanning ecologically relevant sinking speeds. Via high resolution single cell tracking at sea, we map a highly diverse repertoire of microbial motility, including rapid switching between motile and non-motile states. We identify a chemotactic horizon from measured reorientation towards chemical gradients, defining a spatial region around an aggregate within which chemotactic alignment overcomes flow-induced rotation due to sedimentation. This interplay produces a non-monotonic dependence of encounter rates on aggregate sinking speed, with a peak at 14.4 m/day followed by a sharp decline beyond 78.1 m/day, with a tracer-like regime at high effective sinking speeds. We incorporate the measured encounter rates into a kinetic transport equation in position-velocity phase space, with an effective nonlinear damping arising from velocity-dependent remineralization. The resulting particle dynamics reveal a threshold-induced separatrix dividing overdamped and ballistic microbial populations, leading to velocity segregation. Our study connects direct measurements of microbial motility and sedimentation-induced flow to the emergent phase-space for fate of marine snow in the biological pump, establishing a quantitative multiscale framework for investigating ocean carbon export.

papers.title: Chemotactic recruitment offsets congestion in honeybee trophallaxis
papers.abstract: Honeybee colonies distribute food by trophallaxis, a sequence of local interactions in which nectar donors transfer resources to hungry nestmates. Efficient transfer requires a searcher to find a donor and then be served. Chemical signals may draw searchers to a donor, though the crowd they form may block the way. We develop a stochastic framework coupling velocity-jump search that depends on chemical signaling to random-order service at donor aggregations, and measure trophallactic efficiency by the time the colony needs to feed a prescribed fraction of its members. Directed recruitment emerges because fed bees linger near donors and strengthen local chemical cues, but lingering also slows service. Trophallactic efficiency is therefore maximized at an intermediate abandonment rate that balances recruitment against congestion. We determine when displaced cues remain useful and how competing donors partition searchers. With two donors of unequal service rate, the faster one produces fed bees sooner and so advertises more strongly, drawing recruitment toward the donor that can sustain more throughput and away from the one that would congest. Together, these results show how feedback between service and signaling can self-organize recruitment to match local service capacity without centralized coordination.

papers.title: Energetic costs of reaching the physical limits of sensing
papers.abstract: Cells sense chemical gradients by absorbing ligand molecules, a nonequilibrium process that necessarily produces entropy. But how many molecules must a cell absorb, and therefore energy dissipate, to approach the physical limits of sensing? We derive closed-form expressions relating gradient sensing uncertainty to the number of absorbed molecules, which we link to entropy production. Unlike concentration sensing, which depends only on the total count, gradient sensing must resolve the angular asymmetry of the absorbed flux, adding a bounded dipole-contrast factor set by how strongly the cell absorbs. In the strong-signal regime, cells approach peak chemotactic alignment while absorbing a small fraction of the diffusion-limited uptake, with the required number of uptake events set by the relative concentration change across the cell. Re-analysis of Dictyostelium chemotaxis places the cell at 0.25% of that limit with a minor metabolic load, suggesting that sensing is limited by counting noise rather than by energetic cost.

papers.title: Geometric regulation of stress-limited growth on surfaces
papers.abstract: We analyze a model for microbial communities growing on surfaces in which individual growth is inhibited by collective growth-induced pressure. Asymptotic and numerical solutions on the sphere and homogenization of periodic surfaces show surface geometry can be tuned to either slow or accelerate growth. We use these insights to identify classes of surfaces for which the growth rate can be made arbitrarily small or arbitrarily close to the stress-free growth rate. These results show stress-sensing is coupled to surface curvature and topography at scales much larger than the individual, and provide design principles for controlling the growth of stress-sensitive microbial communities.

papers.title: Limits of Cell Sensing in Observer-Absorber Assemblies
papers.abstract: Absorption improves concentration sensing for an isolated cell by suppressing rebinding correlations. We study how that local advantage competes with collective depletion in assemblies of cells coupled through the shared diffusion field. We introduce an observer--absorber model for permeant ligands sensed and consumed intracellularly with finite volumetric uptake rate $\kappa$ that continuously interpolates between Berg--Purcell monitoring and perfect absorption. For a single spherical cell, monitoring correlations, uptake statistics and optimal joint estimator are obtained analytically, and we characterize the transition between using observer and absorber information for sensing. In this case, all sensing strategies improve monotonically with $\kappa$. For arbitrary cell assemblies, we show that the long-time sensing problem can be reduced to solving for just two steady-state quantities for each cell: the mean internal concentration $\Cbar$ and its local sensitivity $\Tbar=-\partial_{\kappa}\log\Cbar$. In multicellular systems, uptake shortens rebinding memory, but it also depletes the signal available to neighbors. We reveal geometry-dependent optima for absorption rates, with Pareto fronts arising from competing objectives, as well as pure observing, pure absorbing, and partially absorbing regimes.

papers.title: A Hierarchical View of Ecological Encounters
papers.abstract: Encounters between individuals, or between individuals and entities like vehicles, are central to understanding a host of topics in ecology and related fields. Problems of mate-finding, predator-prey interactions, pathogen spread, and animal interactions with infrastructure all hinge on encounters. Historically, however, encounters have been difficult to observe at scale, and the relevant theoretical frameworks---which ultimately derive from the ideal gas law---have been badly mismatched to the underlying biology. Here, we synthesize and provide ecological context for recent developments in mathematics, statistics, and physics that permit the inclusion of more biological realism into encounter-related models. We propose an encounters--interactions--outcomes hierarchical framework for organizing core concepts across a diverse range of ecological scenarios. Implemented as a hierarchical Bayesian model, our framework permits tight connections with multi-level ecological data relevant to the estimation of encounter rates and their downstream impacts on interactions and outcomes. Throughout, we emphasize how the ongoing revolution in animal biologging yields empirical datasets that can be employed to quantify otherwise inaccessible rate parameters and their dependencies. We conclude with a series of major open questions about encounters designed to spur conceptual and quantitative integration across models, data sources, and ecological levels of organization.

papers.title: Optimization principles, revisited
papers.abstract: The brain solves a wide range of problems, and some of these solutions are very good indeed. It is an old idea that, in some cases, these solutions may be as good as possible given the relevant constraints. If this is true we can promote this notion of optimization to a principle from which aspects of function and mechanism can be derived, ideally with no free parameters. Optimization principles are powerful and have had many successes, but they remain controversial. We start with a reminder of a classic example---diffraction limited optics in insect eyes---and then a summary of why you should worry about optimization as a more general principle. Next we turn to recent progress on the theory of optimal motion estimation in fly vision, and finally summarize recent results on the landscape for optimization, arguing that (contrary to widely held intuitions) optimal performance need not require the underlying mechanisms to have finely tuned parameters. I hope to convince you that this is a moment to take optimization seriously as the basis for theories of neural coding and computation. This is based on a rather informal lecture at the summer school LASCON X in Sao Paulo, and I have tried to preserve that tone here; pointers are given to more detailed and technical discussions.

papers.title: Transmission and filtering of biological rhythms in stochastic gene expression
papers.abstract: How biological rhythms in upstream regulatory signals are transmitted to downstream stochastic gene expression is a fundamental question in systems biology. Although experiments have shown that molecular degradation strongly influences downstream rhythmic responses, a quantitative theory of rhythm transmission through bursty gene expression remains lacking. Here we develop a general analytical framework based on a martingale-based orthogonal decomposition approach, applicable to arbitrarily complex upstream dynamics. We derive exact autocorrelation and power-spectrum transmission laws, establish an oscillation-efficiency contraction principle, and identify a critical degradation rate required for rhythm transmission. An explicit transmission relation reveals how molecular degradation, burst frequency, modulation depth, and upstream timing variability jointly govern rhythm transmission and filtering. In particular, increasing burst frequency facilitates transmission, whereas uniformly rescaling burst sizes at fixed burst frequency leaves oscillation efficiency unchanged. Applied to the p53 regulatory system, the predicted degradation threshold is consistent with the experimentally observed distinction between pulsing and nonpulsing responses across ten target proteins.

papers.title: Crowding and confinement of mesoscale swimmers in living droplets
papers.abstract: Droplets encapsulating active or living matter provide controllable platforms for studying collective dynamics and active interfacial actuation. However, prior work has largely focused on quasi-2D confinement, microscopic swimmers, or externally driven, non-living droplets. Here, we introduce living droplets internally activated by tens of enclosed mesoscale swimmers to study crowding and confinement in 3D with swimmer sizes comparable to the droplet radius. In large droplets with few swimmers, the droplet oscillation frequencies collapse onto the classical sessile-drop frequency-volume scaling. By increasing the number of swimmers or decreasing the droplet size, crowding and confinement alter the droplet oscillation frequencies and amplitudes as many-body or swimmer-droplet interactions start dominating. We develop a scaling-law framework linking the oscillation amplitude to swimmer speed through collision probability and momentum transfer, enabling indirect 3D velocimetry in the opaque, crowded droplets. Complementary quasi-2D experiments with direct tracking reveal dimensionality-dependent crowding effects, which we successfully describe with a kinetic theory-based model. We show distinct crossovers and strong-crowding asymptotic scalings of the swimmer speed with the dimensionless swimmer density, $U_{\mathrm{crowd}}\sim(N^{\ast})^{-1}$ in 3D and $U_{\mathrm{crowd}}\sim(N^{\ast})^{-1/2}$ in quasi-2D. Our results connect mesoswimmer encounter dynamics to macroscopic droplet mechanics and inform the design of bio-inspired micromachines, fluidic control, and sensing technologies.

papers.title: Kinetics of segregation of topologically-modified ring polymers in cylindrical confinement
papers.abstract: In Escherichia coli (E. coli), entropic repulsion between the two daughter DNA ring polymers under cylindrical confinement is believed to be an important factor governing chromosomal segregation. The repulsion can be enhanced by topological modifications, i.e., by the introduction of internal loops at certain locations along the contour of the circular DNA. However, the effect of topological modifications on the rate of segregation of ring polymers remains unclear. Therefore, we systematically varied the number and the contour length of loops introduced at selected locations by crosslinking monomers. The appropriate crosslinking was motivated by observations that extruded loops are located mainly near the origin of replication (ori-proximal) region of the E. coli chromosome. This resulted in the chains becoming intrinsically anisotropic. Using Langevin dynamics simulations of these topologically modified bead-spring polymers, we calculated the time required for segregation under cylinder confinement. With certain caveats, we found that increasing the number of loops resulted in a decrease in the time of segregation. In line with past work, we propose that this is due to the increase in the entropic repulsion between the polymers upon increasing the number of loops. In addition to the number of loops, the contour length of the loops and the mutual orientation of the (anisotropic) chains in the initial configurations played a role in determining the time of segregation.

papers.title: A hierarchical statistical mechanics approach: hyperstatistics and its applications
papers.abstract: In a recent paper [arXiv:2604.24783v5 (2026)], we have proposed a general approach to treat systems with inherent non-Boltzmann-Gibbsian behaviour at the domain level. Given the high accuracy of our approach and based on the fact that the generalized Boltzmann factor at the macroscopic level embodies a hypergeometric function, we have adopted the term hyperstatistics. We have applied such a statistical mechanics approach to the discharge of a capacitor in a RC series circuit, pressure decay over time during the pumping of $^4$He lines of a closed cycle cryostat, transverse momentum distribution in midrapidity data of $p$-Pb collisions at the LHC, as well as for the distribution of accelerations in turbulent systems. Here, we discuss into more details the ground of hyperstatistics. We demonstrate the versatility of hyperstatistics upon applying it to the velocity autocorrelation function in Brownian motion and also regarding its potential to describe brain dynamics.

papers.title: Depletion Capture and Rayleigh--Onsager Dynamics in Receptor-Mediated Endocytosis
papers.abstract: Receptor-mediated endocytosis requires a particle to approach a membrane in a crowded extracellular environment, form ligand-receptor bonds, and wrap the membrane against bending, tension, and cytoskeletal viscoelastic resistance. We develop a two-stage theory. The capture stage uses the exact ideal hard-sphere Asakura--Oosawa sphere-plane excluded-volume geometry. The wrapping stage combines a spherical-cap coordinate, a quadratic single-mode free energy, a standard linear solid with one internal strain variable, and a two-variable Rayleigh--Onsager (RO) gradient flow. The creep compliance is mapped exactly onto a long-time spring in parallel with a Maxwell branch, preserving both the creep retardation and stress relaxation times. The free energy is strictly convex by its Hessian convexity, and the linear wrapping system has two real negative eigenvalues and an explicit double-exponential solution. Two independent arguments establish strict monotonicity for positive initial drive: the irreducible Metzler structure with its positive semigroup and the interlacing of Laplace poles with positive velocity residues. The first-passage equation has a unique finite root below the unconstrained long-time limit. Normal-cone conditions specify the projected dynamics on $0\le x\le2$, and the projected system retains the Lyapunov inequality of the unconstrained gradient flow. From the same free energy we derive long-time adhesion thresholds, the threshold-minimizing radius, the finite-size window, and the critical cell modulus. The $95\%$ spherical-area criterion is treated as an operational near-complete threshold, with $90\%$, $95\%$, and $99\%$ compared. The capture analysis includes the exact overlap volume, depletion force, Carnahan--Starling pressure rescaling, Stokes approach time, and Brenner wall-drag correction.

papers.title: Before the First Bond: Depletion-Assisted Stochastic Capture at the Onset of Endocytosis
papers.abstract: The first barrier to receptor-mediated endocytosis is not binding but arrival within a few nanometers of the membrane. In a crowded extracellular environment, this pre-contact approach is driven by thermal fluctuations and entropic depletion, yet continuum models usually start from established contact or treat the approach deterministically. We formulate a thermodynamically consistent stochastic theory for this stage. The sphere--plane depletion geometry uses the exact Asakura--Oosawa spherical-cap overlap, not a fitted cap, with either ideal van~'t~Hoff or pressure-only Carnahan--Starling (CS) pressure. Near-wall mobility enters with its essential and often omitted noise-induced drift. The first specific reaction is a Robin radiation boundary; the outer boundary is reflecting or absorbing. Three first-passage quantities are obtained analytically by quadrature: the mean reaction time, the reaction-before-escape probability, and the conditional success time, the last encoded by a Doob transform that exposes the selection bias of conditioning on capture. The local Damk\"ohler number diagnoses the boundary reaction-to-diffusion ratio, while the mean-time crossover follows from the exact reaction and diffusion terms. At baseline, ideal and CS contact depths are \(2.33\) and \(5.95\,k_{\rm B}T\), and the reflecting-outer mean reaction time is approximately \(0.20\,{\rm ms}\); with an absorbing outer boundary the conditional success time is shorter, but the two observables use different boundary protocols. Numerical checks reproduce the analytic results and the radiation-boundary mass balance. This provides a quantitative theoretical framework for crowding-assisted capture before membrane wrapping.

papers.title: Quantum error correction and biological error correction: A structural analogy between qubits and neurons
papers.abstract: We draw a structural analogy between quantum error correction (QEC) and error handling in neural circuits, with respect to their redundant encodings and constraint-based inferences. In QEC, logical information is embedded in a protected codespace within a larger Hilbert space. A set of commuting checks (e.g. stabilizer constraints) is repeatedly evaluated to produce an error syndrome that identifies which constraints were violated without directly revealing the logical state. A decoder then maps the syndrome to a recovery operation that returns the system to the codespace and suppresses logical failure below a threshold. Neural circuits exhibit error-control strategies that can be viewed through a related biological error correction (BEC) pattern: information is distributed across multiple neurons (redundant encoding), yielding reliable collective activity from error-prone unit operations of individual neurons. The structural analogy with QEC raises the question whether collective activity may be constrained on lower-dimensional manifolds (a biological codespace), allowing recurrent circuit dynamics and mismatch signals to function as syndrome-like indicators of constraint violations, driving fast corrective dynamics and slower adaptive updates. Our structural analogy also suggests that new insights into brain-inspired algorithms for collective information processing may inform novel QEC approaches. We perform numerical experiments using simplified models of qubit and neural population dynamics to illustrate the analogy.
